summary: Proposes TFRC-SP, a variant of TCP Friendly Rate Control for applications that send small packets, such as voice. It is for further experimentation only, not widespread deployment. This RFC is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: TFRC-SP adjusts TCP-friendly rate control for flows that send small packets. It aims to provide a similar byte rate to large-packet TCP when both flows experience similar packet loss, but it can be unfair when small packets are dropped less often.

questions: tcp friendly rate control for small packets
subtitle: A small-packet version of TFRC that aims for TCP-like rates in bytes per second.

tldr.problem: Standard TFRC measures its allowed rate in packets per round-trip time. A flow sending small packets can therefore be limited beside large-packet TCP even when it sends fewer bytes per second.
tldr.mechanism: TFRC-SP uses a nominal segment size of 1460 bytes, accounts for packet headers, counts individual losses in short loss intervals, and enforces a minimum 10-millisecond interval between packets.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4828 is Experimental and says TFRC-SP is not intended for widespread deployment in the global Internet. Small packets may receive more than their share when they are less likely to be dropped.

today: RFC 4828 is Experimental. Its text says TFRC-SP is for further experimentation and is not intended for widespread deployment in the global Internet.

sections.title: Why TFRC Has a Small-Packet Variant
sections.content:
TCP-Friendly Rate Control (TFRC) is designed for a smooth sending rate and reasonable fairness with TCP flows using the same packet size. Because its rate is calculated in packets per round-trip time, a small-packet flow may be limited next to a large-packet TCP flow even when it sends fewer bytes per second.

TFRC-SP targets applications that send packets smaller than 1500 bytes and can wait at least 10 milliseconds between packets. Its goal is a byte rate similar to a TCP flow using 1460-byte segments at the same packet drop rate.
sections.plainLanguage: Standard TFRC can limit small packets based on their count, even when they carry fewer bytes. TFRC-SP aims to compare flows by byte rate while limiting how frequently small packets are sent.

sections.title: Rate, Headers and Packet Spacing
sections.content:
TFRC-SP uses a nominal segment size of 1460 bytes by default. If the sender knows the path MTU and the resulting MSS is below 1460 bytes, it should use the MSS; below 536 bytes, it must. The method reduces the allowed rate to account for packet headers, using 40 bytes for the header estimate by default.

TFRC-SP enforces a minimum 10-millisecond interval between packets, which limits a flow to 100 packets per second. A flow that needs to send more frequently must use the conventional TFRC equations instead.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender calculates a byte rate using a nominal packet size and subtracts an allowance for headers. It must also leave at least 10 milliseconds between packets.

sections.title: Counting Losses During Heavy Congestion
sections.content:
Standard TFRC counts a group of losses in a window as one loss event. A TFRC-SP flow can send several small packets in the time a large-packet flow sends one, so that approach could hide repeated losses during heavy congestion.

For a loss interval of at most two round-trip times, TFRC-SP counts each lost or marked packet. If an interval contains N packets and K losses, it uses N/K as the interval length, producing a loss rate of K/N. The receiver still averages over the recent loss intervals.
sections.plainLanguage: During a short interval with heavy loss, TFRC-SP counts every lost packet. This helps a small-packet flow detect congestion instead of treating many losses as one event.

sections.title: Fairness Limits and Security
sections.content:
The RFC reports that TFRC-SP performs reasonably when large and small packets have similar drop rates. When small packets are less likely to be dropped, the small-packet flow can receive considerably more bandwidth, and large-packet TCP flows can be starved in some cases. The memo therefore limits its recommendation to further experimentation, not widespread deployment.

The RFC says TFRC-SP introduces no new security considerations. A transport using it still needs protection against spoofed feedback and incorrect receiver information.
sections.plainLanguage: TFRC-SP's fairness depends on how the network drops packets of different sizes. It adds no new security mechanism, so its transport must protect feedback as usual.
